title: TB7-19587
frame:
Forum: Refugee Appeal Division (appeal tribunal).
Parties: the appellant and the Minister; names are redacted.
Decision under review (from the opening paragraphs): The Minister of Citizenship and Immigration (the Minister) appeals a decision of the Refugee Protection Division (RPD) accepting the claim for refugee protection made by XXXX XXXX XXXX (the Respondent).
How the layers nest here: The RAD member is the author (layer 1). The appellant and the Minister make submissions to the RAD (layer 2). The RPD decision under appeal is layer 3, and what the claimant or the Minister said to the RPD, as reported, is layer 4.

paragraphs.text: The Minister of Citizenship and Immigration (the Minister) appeals a decision of the Refugee Protection Division (RPD) accepting the claim for refugee protection made by XXXX XXXX XXXX (the Respondent). The Minister submits that the RPD erred in its credibility/internal flight alternative (IFA) analysis and findings. The Minister also submits that the Respondent breached the RPD Rules and principles of natural justice by failing to disclose his last Basis of Claim Form (BoC) amendment and by failing to notify the Minister that the witness would be testifying on an issue other than identity. Having found that the RPD did not err in its credibility/IFA analysis or findings, a breach of procedural fairness regarding the amended BoC does not have a material effect on the RPD's decision, and the RPD's decision to question the witness regarding other aspects of the Respondent's claim does not constitute a breach of procedural fairness, I am confirming the decision of the RPD and dismissing the appeal.

The Respondent alleges that he is a member of the XXXX, a sub-clan of the XXXX XXXX in Somalia. His father was the XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX and later became a XXXX XXXX XXXX. The Respondent's father was killed by members of XXXX XXXX regime in 1990. In 1991, during a battle between the XXXX and XXXX clans in Mogadishu, the Respondent was shot in the leg. The Respondent fled Somalia to Djibouti in 1992. He traveled to the United States in 1993 and filed an asylum claim in 1994. His claim was rejected, as were his subsequent appeal and application for the immigration lottery. He entered Canada in September 2014 and filed a claim for refugee protection.

The RPD rejected the Respondent's experiences prior to leaving Somalia as lacking in credibility. However, it found that he had a sur place claim based on his residual profile - as a Somali national from the XXXX clan, having spent 25 years outside Somalia - and faces a serious possibility of persecution from XXXX XXXX XXXX in Bulo Burte. The RPD found that an IFA in Mogadishu is not viable, as the Respondent would not be able to establish himself in that city and would have to live as a displaced person. The RPD indicated that the Respondent's lengthy absence from Somalia and his limited financial resources would prevent him from establishing a network to meet his basic needs. It found that relocation to Mogadishu would be unreasonable considering the Respondent's weak links to the area. SCOPE OF THE APPEAL As held by the Federal Court of Appeal in Huruglica, the Refugee Appeal Division (RAD) is to review decisions of the RPD on a standard of correctness on questions of law, fact, and mixed fact and law, after conducting an independent assessment of the evidence before it.1 The exception to this rule is where the RPD enjoys a meaningful advantage in the assessment and weighing of oral testimony heard, which, in particular cases may attract a standard of review of reasonableness.2 Unless otherwise stated, a correctness standard has been applied. ANALYSIS Procedural issues BoC amendment
The Minister submits that the Respondent breached the RPD Rules and principles of natural justice by failing to disclose to the Minister his last BoC amendment prior to the hearing.

The Respondent maintains that, while his last BoC amendment was re-signed and dated the day of the hearing (July 17, 2017), no amendments were made that day. He points out that the only amendments to the BoC were those made previously and served on the Minister on January 8, 2015 and June 28, 2017. He also points out that the very short BoC narrative amendment that was served on the Minister on June 28, 2017 relates to a fear of persecution in Bulo Burte, which is irrelevant to the issue of IFA, the issue the Minister raised in this appeal. He submits that the Minister's concern about the BoC amendments is unfounded.

I note that one BoC amendment was presented to the RPD on the day of the hearing. The Respondent's BoC narrative amendment dated the day of the hearing3 includes an additional sentence from his previous BoC narrative amendment.4 The sentence reads, "I was shot in the leg". While the Minister may not have been served with the Respondent's BoC narrative amendment dated the day of the hearing, it is inconsequential, as the RPD found the Respondent's experiences prior to leaving Somalia as lacking in credibility, and the additional sentence relates to the Respondent's experiences prior to leaving Somalia.

Further, as noted by the RPD, the Respondent was given the opportunity to amend or correct his narrative at the beginning of the hearing.5 Therefore, even if the latest BoC narrative amendment was not presented in writing, the Respondent could have presented the additional sentence orally at his hearing, before he affirmed that the information in his BoC was complete, true and correct.

I find that the Respondent did not comply with the RPD Rule to provide the Minister with a copy of his last BoC narrative amendment prior to the hearing, and this is a clear breach of procedural fairness. However, since the Respondent could have provided the amendment orally at the hearing, and the RPD found the Respondent's experiences prior to leaving Somalia as lacking in credibility, and the RPD decided the case in relation to IFA, I find that it does not have a material effect on the decision of the RPD to grant the Respondent refugee protection status. A breach of procedural fairness can only be overlooked if there is no doubt that it had no material effect on the decision.6 Witness testimony

The Minister submits that the Respondent breached the RPD Rules and principles of natural justice by failing to notify the Minister that the witness would be testifying on an issue other than identity.

The Respondent points out that neither the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act (IRPA) nor the RPD Rules preclude the RPD from eliciting or relying on testimony from a witness beyond what counsel identifies in a short statement prior to the hearing when proposing a witness. He also points out that a refugee hearing is not bound by strict rules of evidence like a criminal trial where disclosure of witness statements must be given in advance. The Respondent submits that the Minister's representative chose not to attend the hearing, well aware that given the witness is his brother, he may have more evidence to offer than simply affirming identity.

The Respondent also points out that the Minister argues that the substance of the witness's evidence regarding his family ties to his siblings in Somalia supports an error in the RPD's decision. He argues that the Minister cannot rely on the witness's evidence to argue an error in the RPD's decision and at the same time argue that the same evidence was improper.

In my view, the Respondent's argument has merit. I note that it was the RPD who first questioned the witness on issues other than the Respondent's identity, even though the Respondent's counsel indicated in correspondence7 that he was requesting that the Respondent's brother be allowed to testify to confirm the Respondent's identity. I note that the witness was questioned mainly about the Respondent's identity, including familial and clan affiliation. It was not wrong for the RPD to question the witness regarding other aspects of the Respondent's claim, especially considering that the witness is the Respondent's brother and would have knowledge of the Respondent's circumstances.

There is no indication that the Respondent intended to have his witness testify on issues other than identity. It is not indicated in his correspondence, and it was not raised at the outset of the hearing. The RPD was not restricted in questioning the witness solely on the issue of identity, and it decided to question the witness on other areas of the Respondent's claim. While the Respondent was required to provide a brief statement of the purpose and substance of the witness's testimony,8 and the RPD may limit the questioning of a witness,9 there is nothing that prevents the RPD from eliciting or relying on testimony from a witness beyond what the witness was initially proposed to provide evidence on. The Respondent was not in contravention of the RPD rules, and the RPD's decision to question the witness regarding other aspects of the Respondent's claim does not constitute a breach of procedural fairness. Credibility/Internal flight alternative (IFA)

The Minister submits that the RPD was correct in its assessment of the Respondent's credibility: the RPD noted numerous issues related to the Respondent's credibility and subjective fear, confronted the Respondent with these issues, and provided intelligible reasons why it did not accept the Respondent's explanations. The Minister submits that the RAD should defer to the RPD regarding its findings about the credibility of the Respondent.

However, the Minister maintains that the RPD's assessment of internal flight alternative was not correctly made in light of the Respondent's lack of credibility. The Minister submits that the RPD should not have accepted the Respondent's evidence regarding his lack of social support in Somalia and should not have accepted at face value the Respondent's assertion that he had minimal contact with his family or that his family would not be a source of support in Mogadishu.

The Respondent points out that the RPD accepted as credible that he has limited ties with his siblings in Somalia and cannot rely on them as a source of support, and he would as a result be a displaced person. He maintains that, given the requirement for the RAD to defer to the RPD on credibility matters, the RAD must defer to the RPD's acceptance as credible the evidence about his residual profile. He argues that the Minister cannot cherry pick the credibility findings it likes and argue that deference is needed, yet argue that the RAD should intervene in other credibility findings and not defer, without offering specific reasons for why the evidence relating to IFA is not credible. He maintains that the RPD was entitled to reject his past experiences and at the same time accept that his insufficient links to Mogadishu would render him a displaced person.

In my view, the RPD was not wrong to find the Respondent's evidence regarding his residual profile credible. Even if the RPD found the Respondent's evidence regarding his experiences prior to leaving Somalia not credible, it had to assess the evidence which it found to be credible and determine the claim as the totality of the evidence warrants.10 The Respondent provided credible evidence regarding his residual profile that makes an IFA in Mogadishu unreasonable.

I note that the Respondent provided consistent evidence, without omissions, regarding his personal identity, his country of citizenship, and his membership in the XXXX sub-tribe. I note no significant inconsistencies between the Respondent and his witness's testimonies regarding their family members in Mogadishu, or the lack of contact they each had with them.

At the hearing, the Respondent and his witness indicated that their brother, XXXX, an American citizen, had returned to Somalia to get married. They also indicated that he had since separated from his wife and taken ill, delaying his return to the United States. The witness indicated that XXXX was diabetic, had problems with his blood pressure, and had suffered a mild stroke. I gather from their testimony that XXXX would return to the United States when he recovered from his ailments or when he was healthy enough to return.

The Respondent indicated that his sister, XXXX, lives in Mogadishu. The witness indicated that XXXX is uneducated and simply raises her children because the father of her children had died. When the witness was asked if he knew what was happening in Somalia since he communicated with XXXX, he said he did not think she was in a position to tell him the situation in the country, since she is a woman, indigent, and uneducated. In my view, this evidence reveals XXXX incapacity to provide support to anyone other than her children.

XXXX is the brother of the Respondent and the witness. He lives in Mogadishu. The Respondent and witness indicated that XXXX had worked in Saudi Arabia and returned to Somalia with two trucks, some machines, and money. They indicated that XXXX intended to use the trucks and machines to earn a living in Somalia; however, the trucks and machines, as well as $50,000 cash he had earned in Saudi Arabia, were taken away from him in or about 1996. They indicated that XXXX was jobless and did not know where he was residing in Mogadishu. They also indicated that XXXX became mentally stressed and confused when he lost all of his belongings. In my view, this evidence reflects XXXX dire circumstances in Somalia and his inability to be of assistance or support to anyone.

The Respondent indicated at the hearing that he had lost contact with his siblings in Somali. When asked why he had not attempted to maintain contact with them, he indicated that his siblings would expect him to provide them with money or other financial assistance if he contacted them, and he was unable to provide such assistance. Considering that the Respondent has been away from Somalia for such a long period of time and unable to provide financial support to his siblings, it makes sense that he would lose contact with them. The fact that the civil war in Somalia caused many citizens to relocate and caused disruption of communication networks did not help the Respondent stay in touch with his family members. I find the Respondent's evidence on this issue and on the issue of his siblings' circumstances credible, on a balance of probabilities.

The presence of the Respondent's sister, XXXX, and brother, XXXX, in Mogadishu do not undermine the Respondent's profile as a person with little family support. The evidence demonstrates a weak connection between the Respondent and his siblings in Mogadishu. The evidence also establishes XXXX and XXXX incapacity to provide assistance to the Respondent.

The RPD was not wrong to find that the Respondent's residual profile as a member of the diaspora who has lived outside of Somalia for the past 25 years would place him at risk of persecution at the hands of XXXX XXXX XXXX in Bulo Burte. Based on the documentary evidence in the National Documentation Package and the Respondent's residual profile, I find the same.

I also find that it would unreasonable to expect the Respondent to relocate to Mogadishu. The documentary evidence is clear in indicating that Somalia is unable to provide its citizens with adequate state protection. The Respondent is a 50-year-old man who has little, if any, familial support in Mogadishu. Although he has twelve years of formal schooling, it was many years ago, and he has had limited work experience since then. He was a XXXX XXXX in the United States for certain periods of time while he resided there. He has been outside of Somalia for almost 26 years. Considering the Respondent's age, lack of economic means, lack of familial support, and weak links, Mogadishu is not a reasonable internal flight alternative for him. It does not meet the second prong of the test. I find, on a balance of probabilities, that the Appellant has satisfied the burden of establishing a serious possibility of persecution in Somalia. I therefore conclude that the Appellant has established a well-founded fear of persecution under section 96 of the IRPA.

Pursuant to paragraph 111(1)(a) of the IRPA, I confirm the decision of the RPD and dismiss the appeal. (signed) "M. Pettinella" M. Pettinella July 25, 2018 Date 1 M.C.I. v.
